children: , the commercial and military jet-engine manufacturer, dropped about 2.8% to $325.52 Wednesday as Wall Street weighed its $11.75 billion takeover of Consolidated Precision Products. CPP makes the highly specialized castings that have become a stubborn production bottleneck across the jet-engine industry.

GE will fund the deal with roughly $7 billion in cash and assume the remaining debt. CPP is projected to deliver approximately $2 billion in 2027 revenue, with engine components representing about 70% of sales. GE expects demand for airfoils to climb 30% by 2030, so owning more casting capacity could turn a supply-chain headache into a competitive advantage.

The company generated $3.03 billion in second-quarter free cash flow, making the purchase price nearly four times that quarterly figure. Faster component flow could help GE attack its backlog of more than $210 billion, but management must protect CPP's relationships with competing manufacturers and clear potential regulatory concerns. The valuation picture adds another warning: at $325.52, the stock trades 20.03% above its GF Value estimate of $271.19, leaving investors with little room for a messy integration.

title: GE Drops 2.8% After Paying Four Quarters of Cash Flow for One Chokepoint
